title: Time Management Training and Student Stress

scenes.narration: This paper asks whether a short time management training might help undergraduate students feel less stressed and more in control of their time.
scenes.layout_description: A single student sits between a messy clock and a calmer calendar, with orange arrows pointing toward order.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink line art on solid cream #F9F7F2: a university student at a desk, one side cluttered with clock and papers, the other side with a neat calendar; orange and yellow highlights, minimalist, handwritten labels.

scenes.narration: The authors begin from concern about student mental health, citing prior studies that describe stress as common and consequential in higher education.
scenes.layout_description: A campus building looms behind students carrying thought clouds, with one yellow warning circle around the group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Sketch-like black ink campus scene on cream background: several students walking with heavy bags and small worried thought clouds; orange circle around the group, yellow accents, sparse hand-written text.

scenes.narration: They focus on time-related demands, such as workload, time pressure, and self-organized learning, as problems connected with students’ perceived stress in prior research.
scenes.layout_description: Three simple icons surround a student: stacked books, a clock, and a lone study desk.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal black ink drawing on cream: central student holding head, surrounded by stack of books, ticking clock, and solitary study desk; orange arrows point inward, yellow stress marks.

scenes.narration: The gap is important: the authors say research on effective time management training is scarce, especially intervention studies with student samples so far.
scenes.layout_description: A mostly empty bookshelf has one thin orange-highlighted book labeled as a study.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink empty research shelf on cream background, with only a few slim papers and one orange-highlighted study folder; lots of white space, handwritten labels.

scenes.narration: Their research question was direct: can time management training increase perceived control of time and reduce perceived stress among students in this sample?
scenes.layout_description: A large question mark connects a training board to two possible outcomes: calmer face and steadier clock.
scenes.visual_prompt: Black ink line art on cream: training flip chart with a big question mark, arrows to a relaxed student face and a steady clock; orange arrow, yellow highlights, minimalist.

scenes.narration: They hypothesized that perceived control of time would increase, stress measured as tension would decrease, and demands would remain unchanged after training.
scenes.layout_description: Three small gauges show control rising, tension falling, and demands staying level.
scenes.visual_prompt: Sketch-like black ink drawing of three simple gauges on cream background; orange upward arrow for control, orange downward arrow for tension, flat yellow line for demands; handwritten labels.

scenes.narration: The design trained one group, then compared intended outcomes with a control variable, using a non-equivalent dependent variable design from Cook and Campbell.
scenes.layout_description: One line of students enters a training room, then splits into outcome cards for comparison.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink scene on cream: one group of students walking through a doorway marked training, then arrows to three measurement cards; orange comparison bracket, yellow accents.

scenes.narration: The intended outcomes were perceived control of time and tension; the control variable was demands, which the training should not directly change.
scenes.layout_description: Two cards are highlighted as targets, while a third card sits outside the orange target circle.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal ink drawing on cream: three labeled cards, control and tension inside an orange target circle, demands just outside; yellow pin marks, handwritten text.

scenes.narration: Here, tension means perceived stress reactions like mental fatigue, trouble relaxing, and nervousness, measured with the perceived stress questionnaire scale in this study.
scenes.layout_description: A student’s head contains small icons for tiredness, a tense spring, and shaky lines.
scenes.visual_prompt: Black ink line art on cream: close view of student head with tired eyes, coiled spring, and nervous zigzags inside a thought bubble; orange and yellow highlights, sparse labels.

scenes.narration: Demands meant perceived environmental stressors, such as the amount of work and external duties participants reported they had to deal with at that time.
scenes.layout_description: A student stands before two incoming piles, labeled work and duties, without showing them changing.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink on cream: student facing two stacks, one books and one clipboard tasks, with arrows coming toward student; orange outlines, yellow highlights, handwritten labels.

scenes.narration: The training lasted 4 h and focused on prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring task completion as major parts.
scenes.layout_description: A training board displays five simple icons arranged in a neat orange path.
scenes.visual_prompt: Sketch-like black ink classroom board on cream background with five icons: priority star, goal flag, steps, daily calendar, check mark; orange path connects them, yellow highlights.

scenes.narration: Students first reflected on academic and extracurricular activities, then identified which activities mattered most for their study goals and why they mattered.
scenes.layout_description: A student sorts activity cards into a highlighted circle around study goals.
scenes.visual_prompt: Black ink line art on cream: student at table sorting small cards with book, sport, and group icons toward a central goal flag; orange circle, yellow highlights.

scenes.narration: Next, they defined concrete, challenging, proximal goals, set deadlines, planned steps, prioritized those steps, and considered obstacles and ways to overcome them.
scenes.layout_description: A path to a flag includes step stones, deadline signs, and a small obstacle with an arrow around it.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal black ink drawing on cream: path of stepping stones leading to goal flag, small calendar signs and a block in the path; orange arrow curves around obstacle, yellow accents.

scenes.narration: Daily planning asked what to do, when and where to do it, how long tasks might take, and how to avoid distractions.
scenes.layout_description: A daily schedule page sits beside a clock, place pin, task list, and crossed-out distraction icon.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink on cream: open planner page with simple icons for task, clock, location pin, hourglass, and crossed-out distraction; orange boxes, yellow highlights.

scenes.narration: Finally, students were instructed to monitor tasks each day, checking what was completed and what still had to be done that day.
scenes.layout_description: A daily checklist shows completed items and unfinished items separated by an orange line.
scenes.visual_prompt: Sketch-like black ink drawing on cream: clipboard checklist with some tick marks and some empty boxes; student hand holding pencil; orange divider line, yellow check highlights.

scenes.narration: The starting sample was 48 local undergraduates at a medium-sized German university, recruited through boards, newsletters, and seminar invitations with no incentives.
scenes.layout_description: A campus notice board, newsletter sheet, and seminar doorway all point toward a small student group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Black ink campus recruitment scene on cream: notice board, paper newsletter, and seminar door with arrows toward gathered students; orange arrows, yellow pins, handwritten labels.

scenes.narration: For the main analyses, the authors used the 23 participants who completed questionnaires before training, 2 weeks after, and 4 weeks after.
scenes.layout_description: A timeline shows three questionnaire moments, with 23 students highlighted at the end.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal ink timeline on cream: three clipboard icons labeled before, 2 weeks, 4 weeks, with a small group of 23 stick-figure students circled in orange; yellow accents.

scenes.narration: These 23 students had mean age 23.30 years, SD=2.80, studied varied subjects, and about half were female, 52 %, in the analysed sample.
scenes.layout_description: A small mixed student group stands below subject icons, with age and sex details hand-lettered nearby.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink on cream: group of students with icons for different study subjects overhead, small orange age tag and yellow gender balance marker; minimalist handwritten text.

scenes.narration: Most reported no or little experience with time management strategies before training; one reported some more experience, and none quite a lot.
scenes.layout_description: A row of experience bars is mostly low, with no bar reaching the highest level.
scenes.visual_prompt: Sketch-like black ink on cream: simple self-rating ladder or bars, many marks low, one mid-high mark, top empty; orange highlight on low area, yellow accent.

scenes.narration: After training, reported use of time management behaviours showed a nearly significant increase at 2 weeks and a significant increase at 4 weeks.
scenes.layout_description: A three-point line rises gently at 2 weeks and more clearly at 4 weeks.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal black ink line chart on cream with three points, the line rising from before to 2 weeks to 4 weeks; orange line, yellow dots, handwritten labels.

scenes.narration: For tension, trainees reported significantly less perceived stress 2 weeks after training than before training, and also less at 4 weeks afterward.
scenes.layout_description: A tension meter drops from before training to two later measurement points.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink stress meter on cream: needle high at before, lower at 2 weeks and 4 weeks shown as ghosted meters; orange downward arrow, yellow calm marks.

scenes.narration: For perceived control of time, the 2-week result was only a tendency in the expected direction, not a significant increase at that point.
scenes.layout_description: A control gauge nudges upward slightly at 2 weeks, with a small dotted arrow.
scenes.visual_prompt: Sketch-like black ink gauge on cream: needle moves slightly upward from before to 2 weeks, dotted orange arrow, yellow question mark accent; minimal handwritten labels.

scenes.narration: By 4 weeks after training, participants reported a significant increase in perceived control of time compared with the measurement directly before training.
scenes.layout_description: The same gauge now shows a clear upward movement at 4 weeks with a solid orange arrow.
scenes.visual_prompt: Black ink line art on cream: control-of-time gauge with needle clearly higher at 4 weeks, solid orange upward arrow, yellow glow lines, sparse labels.

scenes.narration: Demands did not change significantly from before training to 2 weeks after, or from before training to 4 weeks after training either.
scenes.layout_description: A flat line for demands runs across the three measurement points while other marks stay muted.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal ink drawing on cream: flat demand line across before, 2 weeks, 4 weeks, with a steady stack of work icons below; orange flat line, yellow dots.

scenes.narration: The authors interpret this pattern as supporting that training led to lower tension and higher perceived control, while perceived demands stayed unchanged.
scenes.layout_description: Three result cards are arranged like evidence: tension down, control up, demands flat.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn black ink evidence board on cream: pinned cards showing downward meter, upward clock-control gauge, and flat demands line; orange string links, yellow pins.

scenes.narration: They also note effects seemed stronger for students with no or little prior experience, especially for perceived stress, as shown in Table 6.
scenes.layout_description: Two student groups are compared, with a larger orange change arrow over the no-or-little-experience group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Sketch-like black ink on cream: two small groups of students side by side, left labeled little experience with large orange arrow, right with smaller arrow; yellow highlights.

scenes.narration: The closing message is cautious: time management training might benefit undergraduate well-being, but larger intervention studies are needed for robust conclusions overall.
scenes.layout_description: A balanced scale holds a small training card on one side and a larger future-studies card on the other.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal black ink drawing on cream: balance scale with training checklist and calm student on one side, stack of future study papers on the other; orange and yellow accents, handwritten labels.
